One more question, I was making sure all the parts are compatible and I got this: Some Intel H110 chipset motherboards may need a BIOS update prior to using Kaby Lake-S CPUs. Upgrading the BIOS may require a different CPU that is supported by older BIOS revisions. Any idea what this means?

Kaby Lake CPU were released after H110 chipsets. That means that some motherboards may not support them properly until you update their BIOS. Your board supports them since BIOS 20 which was released late last year. I'm just guessing here, but that RAM you picked is probably (2x 4GB) or (2x 8GB). Unless something changed super recently, DDR is always paired, that's what the D stands for. If I'm wrong and it's only a single stick, you might consider getting a second paired stick, so you don't run into trouble a few years down the road when you cant find a matching 8GB stick. If they aren't matching, you're potentially going to start seeing bluescreen errors.

DDR is always paired, that's what the D stands

It isn't and it doesn't. It stands for double data rate. Meaning it transfers data twice for each clock tick. Once when the signal goes up and again when it goes down. This effectively doubles RAM performance. Software tools can report actual clock frequency or the effective rate. Neither is really wrong.

Dual channel RAM gives you a performance boost so use it if you can since the cost is about the same as single stick but its fairly small, I certainly wouldn't lose any sleep over it.

Right, sorry. I guess I conflated the two, since Dual Channel became a thing (at least in the consumer market) around the same time as DDR. And yes, I didn't mean to imply that he HAD to use 2 sticks of RAM, only that if he ever wanted to upgrade, he wouldn't want to have non paired sticks. Thank you for clarifying.

You're thinking of RDRAM/rambus, that had to be paired and have blanks in the empty slots. Wouldn't post if it wasn't set up like that, let alone getting far enough for a bsod.

Single stick looks fine, leaves room for another 8 later (or 24)

Might be worth it to grab a Ryzen 1600 with 6 cores instead (if you can find one). Hate to throw a wrench into your build like this, but the Ryzen can be overclocked, and having 50% more cores means it's going to be a lot longer before you have to upgrade your CPU, motherboard, and RAM.
For those that don't want to over clock, but use as an all around pc, does it matter if you go with dual or higher, as long as it's 3ghz or higher?

I really don't like Intel's locked CPUs, because even if you buy a CPU and you don't want to overclock it now, you might want to later. Specially when it's about time to upgrade. It's a lot better to say "well I need a new CPU anyways, I might as well try overclocking and see if I can use the one I have a little longer" than to be stuck with a CPU you can't overclock and are forced to upgrade.

Maybe I'm just old school and remember when overclocking was a right, not a privilege you pay for.

For games I don't recommend a dual core. You'll always find youtube videos of people with dual cores saying "look I have a CPU below minimum specs and it runs just fine!", but they're generally not enough, specially in more demanding situations like online multiplayer.

But for browsing, spreadsheets, work, etc a dual core is a very good budget computer CPU.
